title: ptaas-bench score document
description: Output of `bench score` for exactly one run of one tool, and the only input of `bench report`. This is a contract: runners archive these documents, third parties recompute tables from them, so a field is only ever added, never repurposed. Every recall is a fraction in [0,1] or null; null means 'no planted vulnerability was applicable in this bucket', which is deliberately distinct from 0 ('applicable and missed'). The axes are independent by design: reach = the endpoint was touched, exercise = the injection point carried a non-default value, trigger = the oracle fired with proof, trigger_any = trigger plus out-of-band callbacks that could only be attributed by the weak (container, time-window) fallback. `trigger` is the headline; `trigger_any` is published alongside it so a weak attribution is never silently promoted to a proven exploit. `exercise` is null for vulnerabilities with no parameter and is then excluded from every denominator.

schema_version.description: Semver of this document format. Major bump = breaking change for report/runners. 1.1.0 added the trigger_any axis, low_confidence_triggers and metrics.crawl.

generated_at.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of scoring, not of the run.

run.description: Run metadata as recorded by the collector, copied verbatim so the score is self-describing, plus the provenance the orchestrator captured at run open. A published number must be re-runnable from its own record: the image digest actually running for each target and the seeded-state digests read before and after the run live here, not in someone's terminal history.

container_map_available.description: False when the export carries no container/address map. Attribution then never resolves a callback's source address to a target, and a `missing-container-map` warning says so rather than falling back to inference.

containers.description: app -> {service, container_id, addresses, image_digest} captured at run open. Addresses are resolved to apps by lookup only: every target is dual-homed (a correlation hint registered over bench-internal carries a 10.77.0.x address while the callback it explains leaves over bench-public as 10.88.0.x, same container, no octet relationship), and the map is true for exactly one run because addresses are reassigned between runs.

images.description: app -> image digest actually running during this run.

reset_digests.description: app (or '*' when reported globally) -> the state digest read before and after the run. `match` is null when one side is missing: unknown is not a mismatch.

reset_consistent.description: False when any target failed to come back to its seeded state, which invalidates the comparability of whatever ran next. Null when no digest was reported.

catalog.description: Which ground truth this score was computed against. `digest` fingerprints the scored fields of every catalog entry; two scores are only comparable when their digests match.

vulns_in_scope.description: Vulnerabilities belonging to the apps in scope for this run. This is the denominator of `metrics.overall`.

events.description: Raw event counts of the run before synthetic filtering, keyed by event type, plus `synthetic` and `total`.

legend.description: Taxonomy labels captured at scoring time so a report can be rendered from this file alone, years later, without the catalog revision that produced it.

metrics.description: Aggregated recall. Every leaf is a Metric.

by_owasp.description: Edition -> category code (A01..A10) -> Metric. All three editions are always present.

by_render.description: discovery.render. The headline of the benchmark: recall collapsing from static-html to spa-*.

by_requires.description: One bucket per discovery.requires capability; a vulnerability appears in several buckets, so these counts do not sum to the total.

max_depth.description: Longest prerequisite chain present in the scoped catalog (0 = no chains).

chains_completed.description: Vulnerabilities that triggered while every transitive prerequisite also triggered.

chains_broken.description: Triggered while a prerequisite never did. Either the chain is not a real chain, or a prerequisite oracle failed; surfaced, never silently repaired.

vulns.description: Per-vulnerability outcome, sorted by id. Carries the catalog attributes used by every breakdown so the report never needs the catalog.

findings.description: Precision analysis, present only when a normalised findings file was supplied. Matching rules are documented in platform/benchctl/src/benchctl/findings.py.

warnings.description: Instrumentation anomalies, i.e. platform problems rather than tool problems (a trigger with no matching request means an SDK under-reported).

low_confidence_triggers.description: Out-of-band callbacks the sinkhole could only tie to a vulnerability by container and time window. They are counted here and in the trigger_any axis, and excluded from the headline trigger recall. Both totals are repeated inside this block so the gap needs no arithmetic.

credited_only_here.description: Vulnerabilities whose ONLY evidence is a weak attribution; these are exactly the ones that would be over-credited by a scorer that ignored confidence.

unattributed_callbacks.description: Callbacks observed by the sinkhole that no catalog entry could claim: a blind flaw may have fired uncredited.

applicable.description: Denominator. Excludes not-applicable cases (exercise on a parameter-less vulnerability).

recall.description: hit/applicable, or null when applicable is 0.

trigger_any.description: Trigger including low-confidence out-of-band attributions. Never used as the headline number.

route.description: Normalised route template, the form used for reach matching.

exercise.description: null = not applicable (the entrypoint declares no parameter).

trigger.description: Headline: an oracle fired with proof (a sink signal, or an out-of-band callback attributed by token or by signal correlation).

reach_inferred.description: True when reach was credited from a trigger because no request event was observed.

exercise_sample.description: Truncated payload that credited exercise, kept so a human can audit the verdict.

trigger_any.description: Trigger including a low-confidence out-of-band attribution.

signal.description: Opaque metric-shaped identifier the target emits for this flaw. Targets never emit catalog ids (see targets/target-contract.yaml, section deception).

false_positives.description: All findings matching no catalog entry.

ambiguous.description: Findings matching a catalog location but not its class or parameter. Counted neither as TP nor FP by `precision`.

false_positives_confirmed.description: False positives on a route the inventory describes (declared safe, or known but not planted in that shape). These are the defensible ones: we have ground truth for that exact location.

false_positives_unknown_route.description: False positives on a route no inventory describes. Counted, but weaker evidence.

precision_confirmed.description: TP / (TP + confirmed FP): precision restricted to the surface the inventory actually describes.

fp_basis.description: Why a false positive is a false positive, so the verdict can be contested per finding.

host.description: Host the finding was reported against, normalised for comparison: case folded, port stripped, IPv6 brackets dropped so [2001:db8::1] and 2001:db8::1 are one host, trailing dot stripped. See benchctl/inventory.py::normalize_host for why each of those was chosen.

host_match.description: How the host took part in the match. `exact` means the finding's host designates a declared vhost and the verdict distinguishes an exposed path from its hardened twin on another vhost. The `agnostic-*` values record that the host could not discriminate, so the verdict rests on (app, method, route) alone — an assumption that can change a verdict has to be visible.

host_observed.description: The URL authority exactly as the tool wrote it, kept as evidence next to the normalised form.

attribution.description: How one out-of-band callback was tied back to a planted vulnerability.

kind.description: token = a token from our own zone; signal-correlation = the sink registered {signal, destination_host, route, param, request_id} with the collector before its outbound fetch and the sinkhole matched the observed lookup; declared-id = a platform-side emitter named the entry; container-window = only the originating container and a time window matched (a guess).

destination_host.description: Callback destination, which may be the tool's own collaborator domain: the sinkhole is the resolver for the whole target network.

app.description: Target resolved from the run's container/address map, never inferred from the address itself.

source_match.description: Informational: whether the callback's source address also agreed with the correlation registration. A host match is high confidence regardless — a target's outbound address legitimately differs from the one its hint was registered from — so `false` here is a fact about the observation, never a reason to discount the match.

crawl.description: Crawl coverage over the surface each target publishes in targets/<app>/routes.yaml. Reach (metrics.overall.reach) counts only planted endpoints, which is a biased denominator because those are the pages we made attractive; this block counts the whole declared surface, safe routes included. Both are published and neither replaces the other. Empty when no target publishes an inventory.

safe_routes.description: Coverage of the decoy surface. A tool that walks only the planted routes is not crawling, it is guessing well-known paths.

by_render.description: Where SPA crawling collapses, measured over the whole surface rather than over planted pages only.

planted_vuln_reach.description: metrics.overall.reach copied verbatim, so the biased and unbiased denominators sit side by side.

requests_off_inventory.description: Distinct (app, method, route) touched by the tool that no inventory declares, including unmatched requests.

host_resolution.description: `collapsed` means the http_request events carried no vhost, so a request credits every inventory row sharing that (method, route) whatever host it was written for. Coverage of a multi-vhost target is then an upper bound; `rows_sharing_a_route_across_hosts` says how many rows are affected.

hosts.description: Virtual hosts declared by the inventories in scope.
